issues.description: In the Experiment 2 specificity analysis, the token-based result is reported as 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01'. A z-score of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55, making the p < 0.01 claim statistically impossible. This appears to be either a transcription error (perhaps the z-value is wrong) or a copy-paste error from a different analysis. This undermines the reported token-based replication of the specificity effect.
issues.quote: B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the generalised mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects: 'glmer(response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial")'. There is no random intercept for items (nonwords) or for suffixes. With 80 items nested in 20 suffixes, failing to include item or suffix random effects violates the assumption of independence and inflates Type I error. This is an instance of the classic 'Language as Fixed Effect Fallacy'. The effect of condition (B = -1.57) and the graded diagnosticity effect may be spuriously significant as a result. By contrast, Experiments 2 and 3 are reported to include random intercepts for suffixes, creating an inconsistency across the paper.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of words preceding the critical target nonword differs significantly between the congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs. 5.23 words, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). Longer pre-target contexts may independently increase go-past times and regression probabilities due to greater sentence processing load and wrap-up effects before reaching the target. The authors acknowledge this difference but do not include pre-target word count as a covariate in their models, leaving the main effects of congruency potentially confounded.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: The effect of congruency on regressions-out is reported differently in the text and in Table 5. The text reports B = 0.3 and z = 3.12, while Table 5 shows B = 0.25 and z = 2.65. These are meaningfully different values (the z-score discrepancy is substantial), suggesting that different model runs or model specifications produced different results, or that a transcription error occurred. Similarly, go-past time is reported as B = 41, t = 3.837 in the text but B = 43, t = 3.76 in Table 5. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the reported statistics.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01). [...] There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.description: The definition of type diagnosticity states it is 'calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' The phrase 'total number of words falling into this category' is critically ambiguous. If it means the total number of words in that lexical category (e.g., all nouns in CELEX), the resulting values would be vanishingly small for any suffix, contradicting the reported examples (e.g., -TUDE = 1, -IAN = 0.54). If it means total words containing the suffix, the formula becomes P(category | suffix), which makes conceptual sense. The text as written implies the former but the data support the latter. This ambiguity makes the computational analysis non-reproducible as described.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: No a priori power analysis is reported for any of the three experiments. With sample sizes of 46, 29, and 47 participants respectively, and with the critical analyses involving graded continuous predictors (diagnosticity, specificity) tested at the level of only 20 or 30 suffixes, the studies may be substantially underpowered for detecting the suffix-level modulation effects. This is especially concerning for Experiment 2 with only 29 participants and 11 suffixes, and for the diagnosticity modulation analyses in Experiment 3 where the interaction B values are modest.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London [...] Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London [...] 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited

issues.description: Six eye-movement measures are tested in Experiment 3 (skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) with no correction for multiple comparisons. With six tests at α = 0.05, the family-wise error rate is approximately 26%. Furthermore, the diagnosticity modulation is then tested additionally for two of those measures, adding more tests. Across all three experiments, the total number of statistical tests is very large. No correction (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR) or justification for not correcting is provided.
issues.quote: We considered word-skipping, first fixation durations, first run dwell time (sums of all fixation durations during first pass), go-past times, regressions to the target from later parts of the sentence, regressions from the target to earlier regions of the sentence.

issues.description: The authors claim that a regression slope of 0.9 for lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology), being significantly less than 1.0, demonstrates that spelling is more predictive of lexical category than phonology. This interpretation is incorrect. A regression slope below 1 in a bivariate regression reflects the relative variance of the predictor relative to the outcome, regression-to-the-mean effects, and measurement error in the predictor, not a meaningful superiority of spelling over phonology. The correct way to compare predictive power would be to compare mean entropy values directly (reported as 0.61 vs. 0.63, a tiny difference) using a paired test, or to compare R-squared values in parallel prediction models. The slope-based argument as presented is methodologically invalid.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01). That is, the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.subcategory: exclusion of adverbs as a lexical category
issues.description: The computational analysis considers only three lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Adverbs are entirely excluded despite being a major lexical category marked by highly diagnostic and frequent suffixes (e.g., -LY, which has 2,717 entries in CELEX). In the Appendix, -LY shows near-zero diagnosticity for all three included categories (A: 0.039, N: 0.006, V: 0.002), which simply reflects that -LY words are adverbs. This omission means the reported high mean diagnosticity values are inflated — many suffix words that are not nouns, adjectives, or verbs are counted as 'wrong category' entries rather than 'correct adverb' entries. The exclusion also undermines the ecological validity of the behavioural experiments, which use no adverb conditions.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.description: Across all three experiments, only random intercepts are reported, with no random slopes for the within-unit effects of condition or diagnosticity. The maximal random effects approach (Barr et al., 2013) recommends including random slopes wherever the design permits. For example, in Experiment 3, both subjects and suffixes are exposed to both congruent and incongruent conditions; the by-subject and by-suffix random slopes for congruency should be included. Omitting justified random slopes inflates Type I error rates for the fixed effects of primary interest.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: pseudoaffixed word inclusion biases corpus estimates
issues.description: The authors explicitly include pseudoaffixed words (e.g., 'corner' for -ER, 'vanish' for -ISH) because 'there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these.' However, this decision introduces a systematic bias into diagnosticity and specificity estimates. Pseudoaffixed words are disproportionately nouns (e.g., 'corner', 'finger', 'danger' for -ER), which would artificially inflate noun diagnosticity and specificity for suffixes common in pseudoaffixed nouns. The decision to include or exclude pseudoaffixed words changes the meaning of the constructs being measured and the authors do not conduct sensitivity analyses with and without pseudoaffixed words.
issues.quote: We included pseudoaffixed words because there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these (Rastle, Davis, & New, 2004).

issues.description: To test the graded diagnosticity effect in Experiment 1, the authors 'multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model.' This transformation assumes that the relationship between diagnosticity and classification probability is symmetric across noun-diagnostic and adjective-diagnostic suffixes — i.e., that a given increase in noun diagnosticity produces the same change in behaviour as the same increase in adjective diagnosticity. This assumption is not tested. Indeed, the authors find that token-based analyses show the effect only for noun-diagnostic suffixes and not adjective-diagnostic ones (p > 0.8), suggesting asymmetry. The combined analysis may mask category-specific effects.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy in Experiment 3 is reported as '0.86%' with a range of '0.66% to 0.98%'. Given that these values sum to well below 100% only if interpreted as proportions, this should clearly read '86%' (ranging from 66% to 98%). As written, '0.86%' implies virtually all comprehension questions were answered incorrectly, which would invalidate the assumption that participants were reading for comprehension. This is a critical reporting error that misrepresents the validity check for the eye-tracking study.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, 11.7% of data points are missing due to timeouts (2-second response window) or incorrect button presses. This rate of data loss is high and likely systematic: suffixes that are less diagnostic or more ambiguous would generate longer decision latencies and therefore more timeouts. Removing these trials biases the remaining dataset toward items where the diagnostic signal is clearest, artificially inflating the observed diagnosticity effects. The authors do not characterize which suffixes or conditions drove the most timeouts.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: The practice trials in Experiment 1 use the suffix –al, which is also used as a target suffix in Experiment 2 (with specificity = 0.56). Because Experiments 1 and 2 use overlapping participant pools drawn from the same university population (though presumably different individuals), and because –al is also highly relevant to the lexical category judgement task described in the instructions, exposure to –al during practice may prime morphological reasoning strategies that carry over into experimental responding. The authors do not address this potential priming.
issues.quote: Four practice trials were constructed using suffixes that were not used in the main experiment (–ie, –al, –ular, –ling).

issues.subcategory: very low item density per suffix per participant
issues.description: In Experiment 1, stimuli were split into two lists of 40 items, and each participant saw only one list. With 20 suffixes and 40 items per list, each suffix appeared only twice per participant. This is an extremely sparse sampling that makes suffix-level effects (e.g., the graded diagnosticity analysis, which requires estimating a slope across 20 data points) unstable and subject to high noise. The graded regression analyses treat suffix as a continuous predictor, but there are only 20 suffix-level observations, and participant-level data within each suffix are based on two items per person.
issues.quote: Stimuli were divided into two experimental lists with 40 items per list. Participants saw only one list; each suffix occurred twice only.

issues.description: The suffix –AN is included in Experiment 1 as a noun-diagnostic suffix with a type diagnosticity of 0.50. A diagnosticity value of 0.50 means the suffix is equally likely to appear in nouns and non-nouns — it conveys no categorical information. Including this suffix as a 'noun suffix' in the classification task and in the diagnosticity regression analysis is inconsistent with the logic of the study, which is that suffix spellings carry meaningful categorical information. Its inclusion would add noise and attenuate the diagnosticity effects, biasing the analysis toward the null.

Experiment 2 compares congruent and incongruent contexts for suffixes selected for having high specificity. There is no control condition using suffixes with low or near-chance specificity (i.e., suffixes where the target sound sequence has no preferred spelling for any category). Without such a baseline, it is impossible to determine whether the observed congruency effects reflect the presence of specificity or simply a general tendency to use the most common spelling regardless of context. The interaction between specificity and condition is reported, but the absence of low-specificity suffixes limits interpretation.
issues.quote: Eleven suffix spellings that had a high specificity for noun, adjective, or verb lexical category were selected.

issues.subcategory: ecological validity limited by exclusive use of nonwords
issues.description: All three behavioural experiments use nonwords as stimuli. While this controls for lexical and semantic variables, it raises serious questions about ecological validity. In naturalistic reading, lexical, semantic, and contextual information all contribute to processing, and readers would rarely encounter a word that is unknown to them yet perfectly orthographically legal and syntactically embedded. The conclusion that 'skilled readers are highly sensitive to this form of regularity' in their daily reading is not directly supported by the nonword data, since participants must rely almost exclusively on spelling patterns rather than lexical knowledge.
issues.quote: We show across three paradigms (nonword classification, spelling, and eye tracking during sentence reading) that this form of regularity between spelling and meaning influences the behaviour of skilled readers

issues.subcategory: post-hoc selection of type vs. token measures
issues.description: Both type- and token-based measures of diagnosticity and specificity are computed, and the manuscript reports that type-based measures provided better fits to behavioural data in all three experiments. The decision about which measure to use as the primary predictor appears to have been made after observing the results (token measures consistently underperform), yet the token measures are retained in all analyses. There is no statement that the primary measure was pre-specified. The post-hoc explanation invoking contextual diversity (Adelman et al., 2006) is speculative and not directly tested.
issues.quote: A noteworthy aspect of the diagnosticity and specificity data is that that token-based measures provided a poorer fit to our behavioural data compared to the type-based measures, in all experiments.

issues.subcategory: filler items may contaminate experimental effects
issues.description: Experiment 3 includes 40 filler nonwords with verb-diagnostic suffixes embedded in verb sentence contexts. The authors explicitly exclude these from analysis because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' However, the presence of consistent verb-suffix-context pairings throughout the experiment may cause participants to learn or reinforce the general pattern (suffix predicts syntactic role) during the session, potentially inflating the congruency effects observed for the analysed noun and adjective items. No analysis of learning effects over the course of the experiment is reported.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.

issues.description: The paper claims to test knowledge of morphological regularities between spelling and meaning, but the experimental stimuli (nonwords with suffixes) do not allow disambiguation between morphological knowledge and low-level orthographic pattern recognition. The authors acknowledge this in the General Discussion by comparing to Kemp et al. (2009) and Arciuli and Cupples (2006), who found similar effects with non-morphological endings. No experiment manipulates whether the suffix is genuinely morphological vs. a matched non-morphological orthographic string. Thus, the strong theoretical claim about morphological representation is not directly tested.
issues.quote: Our view is that there are fundamental differences between low-level orthographic and morphological cues, in terms of the degree of precision with which the latter are encoded in written language

issues.subcategory: selection bias / winner's curse in suffix selection
issues.description: Suffixes selected for the behavioural experiments were chosen based on having high diagnosticity (≥ 0.50) or high specificity, as estimated from the CELEX corpus. Because these estimates contain sampling error, selecting suffixes based on extreme values produces a biased sample — the selected suffixes will, on average, have true diagnosticity/specificity values lower than their observed values (winner's curse / regression to the mean). This means the experiments are likely testing suffixes that are somewhat less diagnostic/specific than assumed, and also that the graded regression of behaviour on corpus statistics may be attenuated by regression to the mean in the predictor.
issues.quote: These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly argues that English spelling 'has become fractionated' and 'may have evolved' to maximise the transmission of meaningful information. These are causal/adaptive claims that require diachronic evidence. The computational analysis is entirely cross-sectional (based on a 1993 corpus), and the diachronic evidence is borrowed from Berg and Aronoff (2017) without independent reanalysis. Furthermore, selection for communicative function implies a feedback loop between reader behaviour and orthographic convention that is not modelled. The cross-sectional and behavioural data reported are consistent with the hypothesis but do not test it.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.subcategory: multiple lexical categories for same word counted separately
issues.description: The authors create 'separate entries for words that could express different lexical categories (e.g. PLAY as a noun or as a verb).' This means a word like PLAY is counted once as a noun and once as a verb when computing diagnosticity for any suffix it contains. This inflates the effective vocabulary size and may distort diagnosticity estimates for suffixes found on category-ambiguous words, since each such word contributes to two category counts simultaneously rather than being allocated probabilistically across categories.
issues.quote: Separate entries were created for words that could express different lexical categories (e.g. PLAY as a noun or as a verb).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 conducted after unrelated fatigue-inducing session
issues.description: Experiment 1 was conducted 'at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.' This introduces fatigue as an uncontrolled confound that could slow processing and increase timeout rates (already 11.7%). More importantly, the nature of the prior testing session is unspecified — if it involved any language or literacy tasks, it may have primed morphological awareness and contaminated participants' responses in the nonword classification task. The prior session is described as 'unrelated' but this is not documented.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.subcategory: go-past time interaction: trend interpreted as effect
issues.description: In the diagnosticity modulation analysis for go-past time in Experiment 3, the authors report the interaction as significant (B = 28, t = 2.6, p < 0.01) but describe the incongruent condition simple effect as 'a trend towards an effect (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13).' Interpreting a significant interaction whose simple effects are non-significant or marginal requires caution: the interaction may be driven primarily by the decrease in the congruent condition (B = 8.30, p > 0.5 is not even a trend). The presentation overstates the conclusion that 'It takes participants progressively longer to progress past the nonword as suffixes become highly diagnostic in the incongruent condition.'
issues.quote: there was no effect of diagnosticity on go-past times in the congruent condition (B = 8.30, t = 0.634, p > 0.5), whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13).

issues.subcategory: go-past time estimate inconsistency between text and table
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect estimate is reported as B = 41 in the Results text but as B = 43 in Table 5. While the difference is small, it suggests different model runs, rounding errors, or that the table and text were drawn from different versions of the analysis. Combined with the larger discrepancy for regressions-out (B = 0.3 vs. 0.25; z = 3.12 vs. 2.65), this creates concern that the reported statistics may not all derive from the same final analysis pipeline.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) [...] Go-past time | 458 (129) | 507 (125) | 49 | 43 | t = 3.76 ***

issues.description: Experiment 3 uses a viewing distance of 140 cm, which is substantially greater than the 50–80 cm range typical of published eye-tracking reading studies. At 140 cm with 14pt Courier font and a stated character width of 0.3°, the visual angle subtended by text would be very small. This unusual distance may affect fixation behaviour, parafoveal processing, and the number of fixations per line relative to standard reading research, limiting comparability with the literature on eye-movement measures during reading (e.g., first fixation duration norms). The rationale for this distance is not provided.
issues.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm, with this position maintained with a table-mounted head and chin rest.

issues.description: The paper reports multiple experiments with numerous dependent variables, follow-up analyses, and choices between type- and token-based measures. No preregistration of hypotheses, analysis plans, or stopping rules is mentioned. The OSF link contains data and stimuli, but there is no reference to a preregistered analysis plan. Given the large number of analytical degrees of freedom (choice of random effects structure, which eye-movement measures to report, which measure type to emphasise, which follow-up tests to conduct), the risk of Type I error inflation through analytic flexibility is substantial.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.description: The entire computational analysis relies on the CELEX database from 1993 (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993). This database is now over 30 years old and does not include many contemporary derivations, neologisms, or shifts in word frequency. The authors' own example mentions 'Trumpists' and 'Brexiteers' as productive morphological formations, yet such words would not appear in CELEX. Frequency estimates in particular are substantially outdated; more modern corpora such as the British National Corpus or SUBTLEX would provide more representative token frequency estimates relevant to contemporary skilled readers.
issues.quote: We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993)

issues.description: All experiments recruit exclusively undergraduate university students, and no individual differences measures (e.g., reading ability, vocabulary size, morphological awareness, spelling skill) are collected or analysed. Given that the paper's central claim is that 'skilled readers' acquire implicit statistical knowledge of the writing system, it would be important to show that sensitivity to diagnosticity/specificity is related to individual reading proficiency. The current design cannot address whether the effects are stronger in better readers or emerge only after extensive reading experience.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.description: The authors define diagnosticity as 'reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964)' and then distinguish specificity as 'probability of a cue given a category.' In practice, these map directly onto P(category|cue) and P(cue|category and phonological sequence), respectively. The conceptual contribution of calling these new constructs 'diagnosticity' and 'specificity' rather than using established Bayesian conditional probability terminology is not well-justified. The paper does not demonstrate that the labels add theoretical value beyond existing frameworks such as naive discriminative learning (NDL) or cue validity.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964).

issues.subcategory: asymmetric congruent/incongruent context pairings across suffixes
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the pairing of congruent and incongruent context types is different across suffixes. For example, -NESS is tested in noun contexts (congruent) vs. verb contexts (incongruent), while -OUS is tested in adjective contexts (congruent) vs. noun contexts (incongruent). This means the incongruent condition for different suffixes involves different degrees of categorical distance (verb vs. adjective may be more dissimilar than noun vs. adjective). The syntactic frames used for each context type also differ qualitatively (e.g., verb contexts involve adverb placement, noun contexts involve object position). Effects of congruency could thus reflect category-distance effects or syntactic frame effects rather than specificity alone.
issues.quote: Naturally, the pairing of congruent and incongruent context types was different across suffixes (see Table 3 for the assignment of suffixes and their corresponding target spellings to congruent/incongruent contexts).

issues.subcategory: threshold for excluding rare suffixes is arbitrary
issues.description: The authors first extract 154 suffixes occurring in at least 3 different words, then conduct a sensitivity analysis excluding suffixes in fewer than 20 different words (removing 64 suffixes, leaving 95). The choice of these thresholds (3 and 20) is not justified theoretically or empirically. Different thresholds could yield different patterns of results. Moreover, the 59 suffixes with 3–19 exemplars are included in the main analyses but excluded in the sensitivity check, making the main analysis dependent on a large number of very rare suffix instances whose categorisation may be unreliable.
issues.quote: In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged
